The two atomic bombs that the United States dropped on the Japanese cities of Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 and Nagasaki on 9 August 1945, in the last days of the Second World War. They killed between about 150,000 and 246,000 people, most of them civilians. They remain the only nuclear weapons ever used in war.

The bombs came out of the Manhattan Project, the American-led effort that built the first nuclear weapons from the discovery of nuclear fission. By mid 1945 Japan had lost its navy and its cities were being burned by conventional bombing, but its leaders would not surrender on Allied terms. The Allies were planning an invasion that they expected to be very costly.

What happened:

  • Hiroshima's bomb used uranium, Nagasaki's plutonium.
  • Each destroyed most of a city in an instant. Many more died in the following weeks and months from burns, injuries and radiation sickness.
  • On 8 August the Soviet Union declared war on Japan and invaded Manchuria.
  • On 15 August Emperor Hirohito announced Japan's surrender by radio.

Whether the bombs were needed to end the war, and how much the Soviet attack weighed in Japan's decision, is still argued over. The survivors, the hibakusha, became witnesses against nuclear weapons. The bombings opened the nuclear age: within years the Soviet Union had its own bomb, and the fear of nuclear war shaped the whole Cold War.
